title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: I did a three-month clerkship at the Allgemeines Krankenhaus (AKH), the university hospital of the Medical University of Vienna in Vienna, Austria. AKH is the largest hospital in Europe, with about 1,800 beds, and I am told that patients come from various countries, from Western to Eastern Europe, because its departments, medical staff and facilities are well developed. There I did clerkships for one month each in otorhinolaryngology, transplant surgery and orthopedics.

First, I did a clerkship in otorhinolaryngology. Otorhinolaryngology is completely different from the Japanese system of a doctor in charge: it is divided into ward duty, surgery duty and outpatient duty, and although of course the doctor on ward duty sometimes operates and the doctor on surgery duty sometimes does pre- and postoperative rounds, the system basically shares information at conferences and general rounds. I was assigned to a doctor on ward duty, followed that doctor to observe ward management, and spent my time examining patients, drawing blood and discussing cases with local students. I was also free to observe outpatient clinics and surgery, but because outpatient clinics were in German and many surgeries were microsurgery, observing was difficult, so I think the clerkship was mainly on the ward.

In transplant surgery, unlike otorhinolaryngology, there was no doctor in charge, so I had to think for myself about what I wanted to learn and act. At AKH's transplant surgery, kidney transplants are performed once or twice a week and liver transplants about twice a month, and cadaveric organ transplantation is the mainstream. Because the ward is shared with general surgery, I could also freely observe general surgery operations. I attended the morning conference every day, grasped the day's operating schedule, waited in the operating room before the operation I wanted to join began, and asked the doctor directly whether I could take part. In the surgical field I often held the camera as second assistant, and I had the valuable experience of holding the unfamiliar camera while not missing the occasional English instruction amid the doctor speaking German. Also, the sixth-year student rotating with me was very friendly, so when there was no surgery I helped with the first touch of admissions, and I think I had a very fulfilling clerkship.

In orthopedics, as at Nagoya University, it was divided into several teams. I was assigned to the knee and hip team, observing surgery three times a week and outpatient clinics twice a week. In surgery I mainly observed hip hemiarthroplasty. Many of the doctors were very friendly and lively, and I could enjoy the clerkship throughout the month.

Through this clerkship, not only did my medical knowledge and English ability improve, but it became an opportunity to grow in various respects. First, I gained confidence and proactivity to see things through even in an environment where the language barrier exists and where a passive attitude gets you nowhere. Also, the local students were of a very high level, performing IV lines, blood sampling and the first touch of admissions already in their sixth year, and it was a great stimulus.
I am convinced that such experiences will surely be useful in becoming a resident and a doctor from now on.

Finally, I am truly full of gratitude to Dr. 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 and the professors of the International Collaboration Office, who gave great support from the preparation period before the study abroad through the stay and after returning, the professors of AKH, the alumni of the Frontier-kai, the Student Affairs staff, and the many others who gave great support. Thank you very much.
